references.text: In Matthew's parallel account of Gethsemane, Jesus went a little distance from the disciples and fell on his face in prayer ([ref:Matt 26:39|Matthew 26:39]). Both texts describe how Jesus withdrew from the disciples to pray alone.

Mark's parallel account tells that Jesus went a short distance forward and fell to the ground in prayer ([ref:Mark 14:35|Mark 14:35]). This is the synoptic parallel to Luke's description of Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane.
Stephen fell on his knees and prayed, similarly to how Jesus knelt down to pray ([ref:Apg 7:60|Acts 7:60]). The expression "fell on his knees" (θεὶς τὰ γόνατα) is the same in both texts.
Peter fell on his knees and prayed when he raised Tabitha ([ref:Apg 9:40|Acts 9:40]). The same Greek expression θεὶς τὰ γόνατα is used for kneeling in prayer.
Paul knelt down and prayed together with the elders from Ephesus ([ref:Apg 20:36|Acts 20:36]). Again, the expression θεὶς τὰ γόνατα is used to describe the posture of prayer.
Paul and the believers in Tyre knelt on the beach and prayed ([ref:Apg 21:5|Acts 21:5]). Luke repeatedly uses this expression to describe earnest kneeling prayer.
Paul bends his knees to the Father in prayer ([ref:Ef 3:14|Ephesians 3:14]). Kneeling in prayer expresses deep devotion and humility before God, as Jesus showed in Gethsemane.

Isaiah's prophecy about the Lord's suffering servant who was "despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief" ([ref:Jes 53:3|Isaiah 53:3]). Jesus' lonely struggle in prayer in Gethsemane, where he withdrew from the disciples, points to the suffering the Messiah was to endure.

The Letter to the Hebrews describes how Jesus, during his earthly life, offered prayers and supplications with loud cries and tears to him who could save him from death ([ref:Hebr 5:7|Hebrews 5:7]). This likely refers to Jesus' intense prayer in Gethsemane.
